note.note:
Action Plan:
1. Reassured patient that presentation is most consistent with a self-limiting viral upper-respiratory infection; tuberculosis and lung cancer felt unlikely at this stage.  
2. Symptomatic management advised: paracetamol (dose/route/frequency not documented), adequate oral fluids, and rest.  
3. Safety-netting: if breathlessness or chest discomfort suddenly worsens, if new red-flag symptoms develop (e.g., haemoptysis, persistent fever, weight loss), or if no improvement within 4–5 days, patient to seek same-day in-person GP review or urgent care.  
4. Medical certificate (“sick note”) to be issued for a few additional days off work.  
5. Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.

Subjective:
• Presenting complaint: 1-week history of sore throat followed 1–2 days later by a dry, non-productive cough; developing mild exertional shortness of breath, occasional wheeze, and chest discomfort.  
• Symptom course: fluctuating (“better then worse”), initial low-grade fever for ~3 days now resolved, intermittent headaches, reduced appetite but no weight loss. Cough not worse at night. No sputum, haemoptysis, nasal or sinus congestion, rashes.  
• Severity/function: Still able to exercise and climb stairs; required 2 days off work this week.  
• Past medical history: None reported; specifically no asthma, thromboembolic disease.  
• Surgical history: Not mentioned.  
• Medications: None.  
• Allergies: Peanut allergy (no drug allergies).  
• Family history: Mother—lung cancer. No known clotting disorders.  
• Social history: Non-smoker (rare experimental use), no known asbestos exposure, lives in UK >12 years, recent travel only within Europe.

Objective:
• Remote consultation; no physical examination performed.  
• Patient palpated neck—no palpable cervical lumps.  
• No vitals available.  
• No investigations performed.

Assessment & Plan:

1. Upper-respiratory tract infection with dry cough / possible viral bronchitis  
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Acute viral upper respiratory infection / viral bronchitis (DDx “High”).  
   - Differential diagnosis:  
     • COVID-19 infection (DDx “Medium”) – supportive symptoms but no test performed.  
     • Reactive airway disease / new-onset asthma (DDx “Medium”) – wheeze & exertional SOB support; lack of history opposes.  
     • Atypical pneumonia (DDx “Low”).  
     • Pulmonary embolism (DDx “Low”).  
   - Investigations planned: None at this time; advised patient to attend in-person review if no improvement or deterioration.  
   - Treatment planned: Paracetamol (dose/route/frequency not documented), hydration, rest.  
   - Safety-net advice: See Action Plan above; emphasised red-flag escalation.

2. Work absence certificate  
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Required documentation for illness-related absence.  
   - Treatment/Plan: GP to issue sick note covering “a few more days off work.”

3. Health anxiety regarding tuberculosis and lung cancer  
   - Assessment / likely diagnosis: Low probability of tuberculosis or lung cancer given acute presentation and improving trend.  
   - Plan: Provided verbal reassurance; reinforced follow-up if persistent symptoms beyond expected viral course.

Quality checks:
● Missing expected elements: No documented vitals, chest examination, or throat inspection (limitations of remote visit); medication doses not specified.  
● Internal conflicts: Early in consult patient affirmed chest pain; later doctor summarised “you say you don't have any chest pain, as such” – conflict noted.  
● Transcript quality: Clear overall; minimal background noise; occasional overlapping speech.
